inline.s: [Śāriputra, one who purely observes the precepts, one who converts and teaches the donors, and one who is of wide learning and recites the scriptures — that is, one who recites the sūtras, the verses of re-statement, the prophecies, the gāthās, the udānas, the nidānas and the like, the jātakas, the vaipulyas, the events never before occurring, the avadānas, and the treatises — if such a one is also able purely to observe the precepts without flaw, unstained and unclouded, free and unattached, praised by the wise, fully complete in himself, following the concentrations, and always delighting in sitting in meditation — such a bhikṣu I also permit to receive offerings.]

Śāriputra, one who purely observes the precepts, one who converts and teaches the donors, and one who is of wide learning and recites the twelve divisions of the canon — if such a one is also able purely to observe the precepts without flaw, unstained and unclouded, free and unattached, praised by the wise, fully complete in himself, following the concentrations, and always delighting in sitting in meditation — such a bhikṣu I also permit to receive offerings.

[Sūtra, verses of re-statement, prophecy, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, jātaka, vaipulya, event never before occurring, avadāna, treatise]These are the individual names of the twelve divisions of the canon. [Twelve divisions of the canon]All the dharmas spoken by the Buddha, according to the differences in the literary form of the scriptures and in the matters they record, may be distinguished from within the three collections into twelve names, collectively called the three collections and twelve divisions of the canon; in general all scriptures are called “all the scriptures,” and individually they are called the twelve divisions. The twelve are: First, sūtra, translated into Chinese as “the scriptures of connected meaning,” referring to the prose passages in the scriptures that directly expound the meaning of the Dharma, and therefore also called the prose scriptures. Second, geya, translated into Chinese as “re-statement verses” or “responsive verses,” which restate in verse the meaning of the preceding prose passages; such verses are called “re-statement scriptures.” Third, vyākaraṇa, translated into Chinese as “prophecy”; whenever in a scripture the Buddha prophesies the future Buddhahood of a bodhisattva, the future attainment of the way of a pratyekabuddha, the future attainment of the way of a śrāvaka in a later life, or records the future retribution of beings in the other five realms, it is called a “prophecy scripture.” Fourth, gāthā, translated into Chinese as “recollection,” or “independent verse,” which does not depend on prose but directly sets forth the dharmas in verse, such as the Dhammapada; called a “recollection scripture.” Fifth, udāna, translated into Chinese as “self-spoken” or “the scripture spoken without being asked.” Whenever the Buddha himself declares a passage although no one has asked, such as the Amitabha Sūtra, it is called a “self-spoken scripture.” Sixth, nidāna, translated into Chinese as “the scripture of causes and conditions” or “the scripture of dependent arising.” The Tathāgata’s teaching must have its causes and conditions; that is, the circumstances of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma in the scriptures, and the primary and secondary causes of the Buddha’s teaching and conversion, such as the “introductory sections” of the various scriptures — hence it is called the “scripture of causes and conditions.” Seventh, avadāna, translated into Chinese as “parable”; wherever the scriptures and the Vinaya speak of parables, using them to reveal the meaning of the Dharma, it is called a “parable scripture.” Eighth, itivṛttaka, translated into Chinese as “past events,” or “scripture of ‘thus it was said’”; the passages recounting the past deeds and karmic histories of disciples, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas, and the circumstances teaching them to be diligent in seeking the way and liberation — these are called “past-event scriptures.” Ninth, jātaka, this is the birth-story scripture. Whatever passages tell of the Buddha’s own past lives when he practiced the bodhisattva path, cultivating the various ascetic practices and benefiting beings — these are called “birth-story scriptures.” Tenth, vaipulya, translated into Chinese as “extensive”; the general name for all the Mahāyāna scriptures, and also referring to those whose words are extensive and whose meaning is upright, extensively discriminating the profound truth of the various dharmas. Such passages are called “extensive scriptures.” Eleventh, adbhuta-dharma, translated into Chinese as “never before occurring”; the passages telling of the bodies of the gods, the trembling of the great earth, events rare from ancient times, and the inconceivable powers of the Buddha — these are called “never-before-occurring scriptures.” Twelfth, upadeśa, translated into Chinese as “treatise”; if the scriptures spoken by the Buddha are in the form of a treatise, with question and answer, discriminating principles and expounding them at length, they are called “treatise scriptures.”
